proof_summary: A recurrence invariant rewrites the continued fraction as \(B_n(3)/(5n-4)\), so its reduced denominator is \((5n-4)/\gcd(B_n(3),5n-4)\). For each prime \(p\ge7\), choose the unique \(3\le n<p\) with \(5n\equiv4\pmod p\); factorial-sum congruences show that the cofactor \((5n-4)/p\) cancels but \(p\) does not, while a prime-power valuation bound via \((n-1)!\) forces every occurrence to have \(n<p\), giving uniqueness modulo \(p\) (with the \(p=11,n=3\) case handled directly).
